10085-moorish-literature-comprising-roma:
This 1901 collection, translated into English for the first time with an introduction by René Basset of the University of France, gathers the literature of the Moors. Basset explains that the region from Egypt to the Atlantic, and from the Mediterranean to the Niger, was inhabited by the Berbers.

Inside are Moorish ballads and romances, the story of Sidi Brahim of Massat, five Berber stories, poems of the Maghreb, popular tales of the Berbers and Kabyles, and Fatima's love. Readers get North African storytelling in English at last: heroic, romantic, and rooted in a long oral tradition.
10386-thoughts-on-the-necessity-of-impro:
Thomas Clarkson published this essay in 1823, arguing for better treatment of enslaved people in British colonies as a road to final emancipation. Clarkson, a leading abolitionist, first printed the piece in The Inquirer, then reissued it with a candid note that he had overrated recent improvement. His tone is reasoned and humane.

Clarkson shows that emancipation, proposed even by a friend of planters in 1792, is neither new nor wild. He weighs safety, practicality, and advantage, urging gradual reform toward freedom. Readers get a key abolitionist argument, clear on why slavery must end and how it might end well.
10589-turkish-prisoners-in-egypt-a-repor:
Delegates of the International Committee of the Red Cross wrote this report in 1917, on Turkish prisoners in Egypt during the First World War. The delegates visited camps in December 1916 and January 1917, after sailing from Marseilles on the liner Morea to Port Said. Their account is official, careful, and humane.

At Cairo, General Murray put them in touch with Brigadier General Casson, director of prisoners, and Colonel Simpson helped plan visits. A motor car, permission to photograph, gifts, and free talk with prisoners aided their work. Readers get a primary, wartime record of prison camps, inspected by neutral eyes.
10609-english-literature-its-history-and:
William J. Long wrote English Literature as a school textbook tracing the whole story of English writing. It opens by asking what literature is and why it matters, then moves from Anglo-Saxon poems such as Beowulf, through Chaucer and Shakespeare, to modern writers. Each chapter ends with a summary, questions, dates, and books for further reading.

Long stresses the life behind the books: the speech, faith, and history of the English-speaking world. His style is clear and direct, meant for classroom use. Students still find it a helpful road map, and general readers can use it to place famous authors in their periods.
10703-the-history-of-rome-book-iii-from-:
Theodor Mommsen's Book III of his History of Rome runs from the union of Italy to the subjugation of Carthage and the Greek states. Dickson's sanctioned translation follows Rome as it turns from an Italian power into a Mediterranean empire, through the Punic Wars and the conquest of the Greek east. The narrative weighs armies, treaties, and the strain of empire on Roman life.

Mommsen shows how victory abroad changed politics at home, setting up the crises of the later books. His scholarship and storytelling carry the reader through complex campaigns with clarity. Readers get the middle republic at its height, in a work that defined Roman history for a century.
10779-happy-little-edward-and-his-pleasa:
Happy Little Edward, published in 1850, is a picture book for small children about a four-year-old boy's country visit. Edward Jones lives in a Connecticut city with his parents, brothers, sisters, and a kind aunt who cares for him. One spring morning the family sets out to visit his mother's sister, a farmer's wife in Massachusetts.

The book follows Edward's carriage ride and rambles in verse and pictures, urging little readers to wake and follow him to the country. Its tone is sweet and instructive, typical of early American children's books. Modern readers get a charming glimpse of how the 1850s taught city children about farm life.
10810-the-young-trail-hunters-or-the-wil:
Samuel Woodworth Cozzens published The Young Trail Hunters in 1877, telling the veritable adventures of Hal Hyde and Ned Brown across the great plains of the Southwest. Cozzens, who traveled with the boys, says no book fascinated him from youth like travel among Indians, where danger attends every step. A prairie on fire fronts the book.

The narrative records hair-breadth escapes and, from personal observation, the habits and customs of plains tribes Cozzens calls fast vanishing. Its tone is that of a guide turned storyteller. Readers get a firsthand-flavored Western adventure, with the plains and their peoples at its center.
1281-tom-swift-and-his-aerial-warship-or:
Victor Appleton sends Tom Swift to sea and sky with a new aerial warship, a flying craft armed for naval war, which spies and enemy agents try to steal. The tale moves through test flights, sea chases, and a battle above the waves, with Tom's inventions deciding the day.

The book, written as naval arms races filled the news, mixes boy's adventure with dreams of air power. Tom's pluck and his machines carry a brisk plot. It suits young readers who like Swift's formula of invention, danger, and triumph. Swift's flying warship yarn suits young readers who love machines and danger.
1710-la-grande-breteche:
A shuttered house in Touraine called La Grande Bretèche has stood empty for years, and a visiting doctor learns why from local gossip and a servant's memory. The house has stood empty for years. The doctor learns why from a local story: a husband who came home early, a hidden lover, and a wall built in haste.

Balzac tells the horror sideways, through gossip, a servant's memory, and a room that no one will open. The tale is brief but it lingers, because its cruelty is so quiet: no murder is shown, only a door sealed and a woman left behind it. The reader is left to imagine what the silence inside that room must have meant.
1903-everybody-s-guide-to-money-matters-:
William Cotton, Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries, writes a plain guide to money matters for ordinary readers, explaining banks, interest, stocks, and household finance in clear terms. The book aims to help people manage money well. Cotton, a banker and antiquary, wrote for readers with no training in finance.

Cotton describes savings, investments, and the pitfalls of speculation, with examples from Victorian commerce. The guide serves as a readable introduction to nineteenth-century finance, and as a period piece on thrift. His guide explains interest, shares, and wills in language a shopkeeper could follow.
19767-george-borrow-and-his-circle-where:
George Borrow wrote Lavengro and The Bible in Spain, two singular Victorian books. George Borrow and His Circle gathers facts about the man and his friends. One figure is William Ireland Knapp, a scholar of modern languages. Knapp held chairs at Vassar, Yale, and Chicago. He spent eleven years in Spain and wrote Borrow's life. He died in Paris in 1908, aged seventy-four.

Borrow biographies attract odd, devoted scholars like Knapp. Clement King Shorter assembled this circle of lives around Borrow. Gypsies, languages, and Spain run through all of them. The book serves readers who finish Lavengro wanting the real man. It also preserves a vanished scholarly world. Borrow's circle was nearly as strange as Borrow.
20811-two-decades-a-history-of-the-first:
Histories, says Frances W. Graham, wake lost memories and bare hidden events. Two Decades traces the first twenty years of a New York reform group's work. Its shuttle of memory weaves fact and incident into one full cloth.

The Woman's Christian Temperance Union fought drink as a threat to homes. Graham records its New York campaigns, leaders, and wins across two decades. Petitions, meetings, and laws mark the slow grind of reform. The book keeps the voice of those who did the work, proud of ground gained and clear-eyed about how much ground still lay ahead.
21112-the-causes-of-the-corruption-of-th:
John William Burgon, Dean of Chichester, left this defence of the traditional text of the Gospels unfinished at his death. Edward Miller arranged, completed, and edited it for publication in London in 1896 as a sequel to Burgon's Traditional Text of the Holy Gospels. Burgon distrusted the new critical Greek texts of his day.

He argues that errors crept into Gospel copies through careless scribes, deliberate changes, and other causes he sorts one by one. A long section attacks Dr Hort's theory of confluence and the so-called Neutral Text. Indexes of subjects and passages make it a working reference for textual critics.
21240-the-lone-ranche:
Captain Mayne Reid set this tale of the Staked Plain around Chihuahua, a city he says calls up strange records of frontier life. Early cowboy and Indian fiction is what readers get: rough speech, Spanish and Mexican words, and hard riding on the border plains. Reid's characters speak in dialects that fill the pages with non-dictionary words.

The Lone Ranche of the title stands at the centre of the action on the dry Staked Plain of Texas and the Mexican border. Reid helped invent the Western adventure novel, writing from his own years in America. Frontier memory, raids, and ranch life give the tale its colour and pace.
21592-the-art-of-making-whiskey-so-as-to:
Anthony Boucherie of Lexington, Kentucky, promises better whiskey in The Art of Making Whiskey, printed there in 1819. His full title pledges a purer, cheaper spirit, and more of it, from the same grain. A second art turns that spirit into gin, after the Dutch method.

The work was translated from Boucherie's French by a hand masked as C. M. It was entered at law in December 1818, in the district of Kentucky. Copies survive only in poor shape, and the editors kept the printer's errors marked. Early American distilling gets a rare, close record in these pages.
22207-the-romance-of-giovanni-calvotti-f:
The Romance of Giovanni Calvotti comes from David Christie Murray's story set Coals of Fire. Calvotti introduces himself with unusual candour. He is an Italian and a gentleman, aged thirty. His main fault, he says, is being able to do much in too many directions. Music, verse in four languages, and composition all show his great undeveloped talent.

Murray lets the man's vanity narrate its own undoing. Calvotti's romance tests whether brilliance without ballast can win or keep love. The tale is part character study, part cautionary comedy. Among the Coals of Fire stories it shows Murray's lighter, more ironic touch.
22547-the-rover-boys-on-treasure-isle-or:
The Rover Boys on Treasure Isle sends three brothers on a strange cruise. The subtitle names the steam yacht that carries them south. In his preface, the author recalls the series' long run with readers.

Years ago the first three volumes began the Rover Boys' adventures. They were The Rover Boys at School and On the Ocean. The Rover Boys in the Jungle completed that first trio. At that time, he thought to end with a fourth volume. Readers wanted more, so the brothers kept sailing onward. Treasure Isle promises buried wealth and a curious voyage together. The Rovers remained models of pluck for American boys. This cruise delivers sea adventure in the series' brisk style.
23003-the-new-minister-s-great-opportuni:
A villager prices sermons in The New Minister's Great Opportunity, a story by Heman White Chaplin first published in a magazine. I don't see much job in that, the man says. A pastor already owes two sermons a week, the man reckons, with an endless supply behind them. One extra sermon costs nothing, since the stock is free. It's like wheeling gravel from the pit.

That dry arithmetic frames the minister's chance when it comes. Chaplin's coastal people test their new pastor with the same plain sense they apply to fish and freight. Faith, in his stories, must survive the store's counter talk. The humor is dry as salt cod. Readers get a small, perfect specimen of his village manner.
23029-ohio-arbor-day-1913-arbor-and-bird:
Ohio's governor signs off in the Ohio Arbor Day 1913 manual. The proclamation closes in full legal form. At Columbus in mid-January 1913, the governor signs his name and orders the state's Great Seal attached.

The manual that follows arms teachers for Arbor and Bird Day. Programs, poems, tree-planting directions, and bird lore fill it, all meant for schoolrooms across the state. Ohio took the holiday seriously, and print like this carried the observance into one-room schools. The booklet preserves a whole civic ritual of the Progressive Era. Trees, birds, children, and the state seal share its pages in perfect confidence.
2390-the-conquest-of-the-old-southwest-t:
Archibald Henderson tells the romantic story of the Old Southwest: the Carolinas, Tennessee, and Kentucky from 1740 to 1790, when pioneers crossed the mountains into a contested land. The Conquest of the Old Southwest follows Boone, Robertson, and Sevier through wars with Native peoples, land hunger, and the founding of new settlements. Henderson writes with the sweep of a popular historian.

The book's older view of frontier heroism now needs balancing with Native perspectives, but its narrative energy endures. It preserves the pioneer legends as Americans once told them. Readers of frontier history will find a vivid account.
2476-the-circus-boys-in-dixie-land-or-wi:
The Circus Boys take their show to Dixie Land in this volume, winning plaudits from Southern crowds as they perform under new skies. Edgar B. P. Darlington follows the young aerialists through Southern towns, with fresh rivals, mishaps, and the particular color of the road in the South. The circus itself remains the hero.

The story's travelogue flavor adds to its adventure, as the boys learn new audiences and new tricks. Series readers will enjoy the change of scene. It is a cheerful, fast-moving boys' book. Darlington's series ran to many volumes following the same young performers.
3003-wild-flowers-an-aid-to-knowledge-of:
Neltje Blanchan wrote Wild Flowers, also published as Nature's Garden, as a guide to knowing North American wildflowers in the field. The book describes each flower by family, color, season, and habit, so a walker can name what grows beside the path. Entries give size, scent, and leaf shape in plain language rather than technical keys alone.

A trailing arbutus entry, for example, notes pink flowers fading to nearly white, very fragrant, about half an inch across, in few or many clusters. Another describes a straggling bush lower than lambkill, blooming in June with deep rose or lilac clusters. The book remains a friendly introduction to flower study, written for readers who walk and look.
3430-the-suitors-of-yvonne-being-a-porti:
Rafael Sabatini presents this romance as part of the memoirs of a French adventurer in the age of Cardinal Mazarin. The chapter titles tell the shape of the plot: a boy drinks too much wine, a fight breaks out in the horse market, fair rescuers intervene, and Mazarin himself turns matchmaker. Love sickness, a whip used as argument, and a rescue follow.

At the center stands Yvonne, courted by rival suitors while her family and the Cardinal maneuver around her. The narrator's fortunes rise and fall with duels, disguises, and sudden reversals. Sabatini writes with speed and color, and the book suits readers who like cloak and sword romance set among real figures of seventeenth century France.
3731-disturbances-of-the-heart-discussio:
Oliver Osborne wrote this medical book for doctors facing the most common grave illness of his day, disease of the heart. It works through the organ chamber by chamber, valve by valve, and explains how narrowed openings, stiffened cusps, and scarred tissue change the way blood moves. Each fault gets its signs at the bedside, its course over time, and the treatment then in use, with diet, rest, and drugs weighed in turn.

Long passages deal with endocarditis, the inflammation of the heart lining that often follows acute illness and may heal without a trace or may leave a valve unable to open or close. Osborne writes in a plain clinical style, with cases rather than theory in the foreground. The book now serves as a record of cardiology before modern surgery, useful to students of medical history and to curious lay readers with patience for detail.
4629-home-scenes-and-home-influence-a-se:
T. S. Arthur published Home Scenes, and Home Influence in 1854, as the fifth volume in Arthur's Library for the Household. His preface says many scenes show a mother's influence with her children, a few include the marriage relation, and a few give other domestic pictures. In all, readers should find motives for self-denial and right action in the various conditions of social life, since home is the centre of good as well as bad influence.

Contents include Taking Comfort, Children, Losing One's Temper, and Trouble with Servants. They go on to Old Maids' Children, The Mother and Boy, The Christmas Party, Is She a Lady?, A Mother's Influence, and The Power of Patience. Arthur argues that those trusted with the home-circle hold its true power over the heart. Readers get a set of short domestic tales, warm and instructive, for family reading.
6426-dick-prescott-s-first-year-at-west-:
H. Irving Hancock, in a 1910 Saalfield book, follows Dick Prescott and Greg Holmes through a first year at West Point in cadet grey. Two tiny specks of nothing opens the tale, as Greg whispers to Dick, asking how he feels, spruce as an hour ago, with a half nervous laugh. The tyranny of the cadet corporal, lucky ones taking up new life, and Greg's blues follow.

Candidate Dodge is critical, yearling hazers take the plebes in hand, and a sudden grind at math, Dick's trouble, and a first fight test the chums. Dodge holds post number three, Prescott gets it, a sentry makes a capture, and Greg overhears a pretty girl's tribute. Hancock writes boy's military school life with drill, hazing, and friendship, where two chums learn to stand their ground together.
6427-the-story-of-rome-from-the-earliest:
Arthur Gilman rehearses Rome's lustrous story from myth and fable's mists to the republic's mischievous end, just before empire's brilliant period opens. Once upon a time, Troy's old king, Paris the wayward youth, Helen carried off, and a ten year war lead to Aeneas, son of Anchises, sailing to Italy. Fact and fiction shade into each other in early stories, as Milton, Virgil, and Livy each retell Aeneas in turn.

Shepherds begin the city, with Romulus and Remus on two hills, vultures deciding, Pales god of shepherds, and an asylum for bachelors wanting wives. A game of wife snatching, Sabines wanting daughters back, and Tarpeia on the hill follow. Later, Icilius holds a loved one's body before the forum people, crying Appius's work, and tumult drives Appius home. Gilman writes Rome for young readers, as story first and history second.
6608-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
On and near the Delaware, Skinner turns to war ghosts and brave deeds from the Revolution. A phantom dragoon rides Iron Hill near Newark, where British tents once stood before Brandywine, and a phantom drummer and a missing soldier of Valley Forge follow. Tales of Germantown, Brandywine, and Printz Hall mix battle with haunting.

A Tory's change of heart, a Bible that saves a life, and a father's dream all show how lore grew from real fear and faith. Skinner keeps each tale short and place-bound, so the Delaware country itself feels like a character. This third volume is a fine mix of history, ghost story, and local pride.
6632-a-popular-history-of-ireland-from-t:
Thomas D'Arcy McGee tells Ireland's story in volume one, from the earliest period to the point where volume two takes up the tale. His publishers' preface paints Ireland rising from dust, drying her tears, and claiming her place among nations. For five hundred years, they say, her life seemed put out, save for a flash of old spirit now and then.

McGee writes as a champion of Ireland, keen to show a fame that spread wide before England's flag even flew. The history that follows is popular in style, meant for wide reading rather than for scholars alone. Volume one lays the ground for the long struggle toward Catholic emancipation.
6633-a-popular-history-of-ireland-from-t:
Volume two of McGee's Irish history picks up at book eight, chapter four, with Sir Henry Sidney's deputyship and the parliament of 1569. The second Geraldine League, the undertakers in Ulster and Leinster, and the plantation of Munster follow in quick, troubled succession. Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, and Hugh Roe O'Donnell rise as the tale moves toward war.

Glenmalure, the Spanish Armada, and the Ulster confederacy fill the later chapters, with campaigns, talks, and escapes. McGee keeps the narrative vivid and partisan, on Ireland's side throughout. Volume two carries the story through its hardest years, toward the long fight for faith and land.
6634-a-popular-history-of-ireland-from-t:
McGee's complete history runs from Ireland's earliest period through to Catholic emancipation, in twelve books rather than in separate volumes. The same proud preface opens it: Ireland lifting herself from dust and tears to claim her place among nations, after centuries when her life seemed put out. This longer text carries the tale past the break that ends volume one.

Readers get the full arc in one place, from ancient fame through oppression, revolt, and the slow road to emancipation. McGee writes with passion and a popular touch, for readers who want a story, not a dry chronicle. The complete history is the best single-volume path through his Irish epic.
7126-the-treaties-of-canada-with-the-ind:
Alexander Morris, late chief officer of Manitoba, the North West lands, and Keewatin, sets down Canada's treaties with the Indians of Manitoba and the North West lands, with the talks behind them. He gives the book to the Earl of Dufferin, ambassador at St Petersburg, moved by Dufferin's keen care for winning Indian friendship and for tribal welfare in the Canadian North West.

Dufferin also backed opening the lands for new homes, by gaining the tribes' fair gift of title to the rich belt on just terms. Morris writes by kind leave, in honor of that care. The book keeps treaty texts, talks, and related notes, as a record of Crown and peoples making terms on a moving frontier.
7210-the-motor-girls-on-waters-blue-or-t:
Margaret Penrose's Motor Girls on Waters Blue opens with a car swinging into a gravel drive, brakes whining. A sun-bronzed girl lifts gloved hands from the wheel after a fast, glorious run. She locks the ignition, pauses on the bottom step, and gazes over the valley below the high-set house, tired and happy from the drive.

That motor energy soon turns to water, as the strange cruise of the Tartar promised by the title draws the girls from road to lake or sea. Penrose writes brisk, outdoor adventure for young readers, full of motion, friendship, and pluck. The opening run sets the pace for a tale where girls drive the action themselves.
7387-grisly-grisell-or-the-laidly-lady-o:
Charlotte M. Yonge sets this historical tale in the Wars of the Roses, opening with a terrible shriek and an explosion in the great manor house at Amesbury. The heroine is Grisell, the laidly lady of Whitburn, whose story unfolds against the shifting fortunes of York and Lancaster. Yonge takes a Chaucer epigraph on women's steadfastness as her keynote.

Through danger, disgrace, and long patience, Grisell endures what the wars throw at her house and kin. Yonge, famous for family chronicles like The Heir of Redclyffe, writes here with the same moral seriousness, but in a more romantic key. The book offers a Victorian retelling of medieval England: castles and battles on the surface, and underneath, a study of loyalty held firm under pressure.
7444-psyche:
Molière's Psyche is a tragédie-ballet, a play with music and dance, telling the myth of Psyche and Love. Molière sketched the plan, wrote the prologue, the first act, and the opening scenes of the second and third acts, when the king asked for the play finished before Lent. Pierre Corneille, then sixty, helped and wrote the remaining scenes in a fortnight, while Quinault supplied the songs.

Charles Heron Wall's translation gives the play in English prose, with short introductions and notes. Jupiter, Venus, Love, and Zephyr appear among the persons, and Molière himself once played Zephyr on stage. The result is a rare glimpse of two great French dramatists at work together, turning a classical love story into court spectacle.
7489-through-central-borneo-an-account-o:
Carl Lumholtz, a Norwegian explorer and member of the Society of Sciences of Christiania, spent two years traveling through Central Borneo between 1913 and 1917. He had long wanted to explore the island's interior, large tracts of which were still unknown to the outside world. His project grew to cover other regions of Dutch Borneo as well. The book carries his own photographs and a map.

Lumholtz had camped before with the aborigines of Queensland, and he approached Borneo's peoples, called in the subtitle the land of the head-hunters, with the same patient curiosity. He records their customs, crafts, and daily life, quoting Wallace's judgment that the better specimens of savages surpass the lower examples of civilized peoples. The account is a classic of early ethnographic travel.
7494-the-outdoor-girls-in-army-service-o:
Laura Lee Hope, author of the Bobbsey Twins and the Moving Picture Girls, sent her Outdoor Girls to war work in this 1918 volume. Mollie, Grace, and their friends volunteer, knit sweaters for soldiers, and face grim shadows of war and news from the front. Grace's knitting draws teasing from Mollie, who fishes in vain for a lost stitch and doubts the soldiers would fare well on Grace's sweaters.

The girls' service leads them to a powder mill, a shot in the dark, moonlight and mystery, a robbery, and a spy again and again. Honor flags, a hostess house, and helping Uncle Sam fill the later chapters. The book is a home-front adventure for young readers, full of pluck and patriotism, written while the war it describes was still being fought.
8329-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-29-lame:
Jerusalem has fallen, and these five poems weep over it. Lamentations, linked to Jeremias in the Douay-Rheims tradition, walks the ruined streets in the first poems: a city once full of people now sits alone, its gates broken, its children hungry. The middle poem, the longest, turns personal, as a sufferer speaks of affliction and then of mercies new every morning.

The poems are built with care, the first four in alphabetical acrostics, as if grief itself needed order. The last poem is a communal prayer, asking God to remember and restore. Short enough to read in one sitting, Lamentations gives sorrow a shape and a voice, and Jews still read it on the fast day marking the temple's destruction.
8773-birth-control-a-statement-of-christ:
Halliday G. Sutherland, a Edinburgh physician, argues the Christian case against the neo-Malthusians in this book on birth control. His first chapter attacks the essential fallacies of Malthusian teaching: that population grows geometrically while food grows arithmetically, that overpopulation causes poverty and disease, and that such teaching rests on false premises. He finds no evidence of overpopulation in the Suez Canal Zone or in closed countries like Japan, and points to a natural law checking fertility.

Later chapters develop a Catholic moral argument against artificial birth control, defending marriage, family, and the natural order as Sutherland understands them. The book is a direct reply to Margaret Sanger and her allies, and it shows the other side of a fierce 1920s debate. Readers should approach it as a historical polemic, valuable for understanding religious opposition to birth control in its own terms.
8815-narrative-of-captivity-in-abyssinia:
Henry Blanc, staff assistant-surgeon of the Bombay Army, lately on special duty in Abyssinia, writes this narrative of captivity under Emperor Theodore. An account of the emperor, his country, and his people. Early chapters trace Theodore's rise and conquests, his army and administration, the causes of his fall, and his personal appearance, character, household, and private life. Europeans in Abyssinia follow: Bell and Plowden, Consul Cameron, French envoys, the Gaffat people, and Mr Stern's mission.

Imprisonment, negotiations, and the British expedition that ended the captivity form the narrative core. Blanc writes as a medical officer and eyewitness, with detail on Ethiopian court life and on the prisoners' suffering. The book remains a key firsthand source on Theodore's Ethiopia and on Victorian Britain's most famous African rescue, readable as adventure and as history at once.
9550-manual-of-gardening-second-edition-:
L. H. Bailey, a noted American plant scientist, issued the second edition of his Manual of Gardening in 1910. The book guides home owners in making grounds and growing flowers, fruits, and vegetables for home use. It starts with the point of view: a garden should form a picture, not a jumble of beds. Plans, walks, lawns, and borders all serve that whole design.

Later chapters take up grading, terraces, trees, flower borders, and seasonal tasks through the year. Bailey stresses form and leaf as much as bloom, and warns against odd beds that spoil the scene. A reader gets a sound, plain handbook for a home garden, still wise on design, soil, and the year's round of work.
9564-among-the-hills-and-other-poems-par:
Part five of Whittier's Narrative and Legendary Poems leads with Among the Hills, a long idyll of New England country life. Whittier first printed the poem as The Wife in the Atlantic Monthly in January 1868, then filled it out for book form that December. He dedicated it to Annie Fields, wife of publisher James T. Fields. The part also holds The Dole of Jarl Thorkell, The Two Rabbins, and Noremega.

Other poems here include Miriam, Maud Muller, Mary Garvin, and The Ranger, each a compact tale in verse. Whittier's voice stays plain and earnest, rooted in farm, faith, and home. A reader gets some of his most loved narrative verse, with country scenes that still feel fresh and clear.
9592-personal-sketches-and-tributes-part:
Part two of volume six of Whittier's works holds his personal sketches and tributes to friends and public men. The Funeral of Torrey opens, honoring Charles T. Torrey, a young minister who died in a Maryland jail in 1846 for aiding runaway slaves. Later sketches salute Edward Everett, Lewis Tappan, Bayard Taylor, and William Ellery Channing. Lydia Maria Child and Oliver Wendell Holmes also appear.

Other pieces mark the death of President Garfield, recall old Newbury, and praise Edwin Percy Whipple. Whittier writes with grief, praise, and moral fire, as one who knew these folk. A reader gets a moving gallery of reformers and writers, seen through the eyes of a friend.
9599-the-works-of-john-greenleaf-whittie:
Volume seven of Whittier's works closes the set with his prose on slavery, politics, the inner life, and criticism. The Conflict with Slavery leads, from justice and expediency to the founding of the Anti-Slavery Society. Reform and Politics follows, with woman suffrage, Indian civilization, and arbitration. The Inner Life and Criticism complete the volume.

Taken whole, the book shows Whittier the essayist at full stretch, from abolition to poetry reviews. His prose stays plain, moral, and warm. A reader gets the capstone of Whittier's works, where a poet's public and private mind meet in one volume.
984-who-was-who-5000-b-c-to-date-biograp:
An anonymous editor, Irwin L. Gordon, compiled this biographical dictionary, Who Was Who, 5000 B.C. to Date, of the famous and of those who wanted to be. Entry requires proof that the person has died; notices from press agents are turned away.

The entries mix real fame with satire, poking fun at vanity, obituary puff, and the hunger for a place in history. The book is a joke with a sharp edge, a mock reference work for readers who enjoy seeing pomposity deflated. It charms as a period piece of American humour, where death alone earns an entry.
9907-the-raid-from-beausejour-and-how-th:
Charles G. D. Roberts joined two stories of Acadia in this book: a raid from Beauséjour and a family's fight to lift a mortgage. The first tale opens with the cry that Beaubassin must go, and follows Pierre to the English lines as French and English forces prepare for a midnight march.

The second story turns from war to home, where the Carter boys work to save their family's farm from debt. Roberts, a Canadian writer, grounds both tales in the woods, forts, and villages of old Acadia. Readers get action and hardship side by side, in a corner of colonial history often left out of schoolbooks.
a-popular-history-of-ireland-from-the-ea:
Thomas D'Arcy McGee tells Ireland's story in two volumes, and this first volume begins with the publishers' preface picturing Ireland lifting herself from the dust to demand her place among the nations. Book one covers the first inhabitants, the first ages, and Christianity preached at Tara, then the constitution and how the kings kept it.

Chapters follow the Irish schools and saints of the first Christian centuries, the Danish invasion, the reigns of Flan of the Shannon and Malachy, and Brian's rise to the battle of Clontarf. McGee writes as scholar and patriot together, from the records and the sagas alike. This volume carries the tale through the age of the Northmen; the second takes it to Catholic Emancipation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-absinthe:
Absinthe here is not the liquor but the biblical plant wormwood, Hebrew la'anah, known for repulsive bitterness. Scripture cites it in Jeremiah, Deuteronomy, Lamentations, and Proverbs. As a figure it denotes curse or calamity, and injustice in Amos. In Apocalypse 8:11 the Greek equivalent names the star that dropped into the waters, turning them bitter.

Jerome's Vulgate gives absinthium for the Hebrew word, except in Deuteronomy 29:18, where it gives amaritudo. The biblical plant seems identical with Artemisia monosperma, Artemisia herba-alba, or Artemisia judaica. The entry points readers to its companion piece on plants in the Bible and cites Hagen, Vigouroux, and Tristram.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alanus-de-rup:
Alanus de Rupe, sometimes Alain de la Roche, was born about 1428 and died at Zwolle in Holland on 8 September 1475. Some claim him German, others Belgian, but his disciple Cornelius Sneek says he was born in Brittany. Entering the Dominican Order early in life, he distinguished himself at Saint Jacques, Paris, in philosophy and theology.

Teaching from 1459 to 1475 took him to Paris, Lille, Douay, Ghent, and Rostock, where in 1473 he became Master of Sacred Theology. Sixteen years of teaching made him a renowned preacher. Indefatigable in his special mission, preaching and re-establishing the Rosary, he succeeded across northern France, Flanders, and the Netherlands. Dated 1460 is his vision of restoring the Rosary. He published nothing in life, but after his death his province's brethren collected his writings. His relations of St. Dominic's visions and sermons, supposedly revealed to Alanus, count as unhistorical.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandre-ant:
Alexandre-Antonin Taché was the first Archbishop of St. Boniface in Manitoba, a missionary, prelate, and writer of Canada, born at Fraserville in Quebec in July 1823 and dead at St. Boniface in June 1894. His father belonged to a Canadian family, and through his mother he descended from La Vérendrye, the explorer of the country of his life's work. He studied at the College of St. Hyacinthe, joined the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, and reached St. Boniface in August 1845.

Taché was ordained a priest at St. Boniface in October 1845 and laboured in the north. He learned Saulteux, then Chippewayan, at Ile-à-la-Crosse. After Bishop Provencher's death in 1853 he carried on his missions. A later division let him attend to the missions and parishes of Assiniboia, now Manitoba. Called home from the Vatican Council, he saw the promised amnesty refused after Scott's execution, a blow to his standing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-campeche:
Campeche is a diocese in Mexico, under Yucatán, created on 24 March 1895 by dividing the Diocese of Yucatán. Its land covers the western Yucatán peninsula, with plains in the north, broad savannahs and dense forests, and a well-watered south. Spaniards found a Maya seaside village called Ah Kin Pech in 1517. In 1540 Captain Montejo founded a seaport town there, starting at once the church of Santa Maria de la Concepción, now the cathedral.

The first bishop to visit Campeche was Bartolomé de las Casas, driven ashore by a storm, and its first missionaries were Franciscans, followed by Jesuits in 1715 until their expulsion in 1767. The diocese counts about 100,000 people in twenty-three parishes, and its third bishop, Francisco Mendoza y Herrera, opened a seminary, three colleges, and an episcopal residence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-rothe:
A biographical entry presents David Rothe, Bishop of Ossory in Ireland, born at Kilkenny in 1573 and dead on 20 April 1650. Schooled at Douai and Salamanca, he took a doctorate in civil and canon law. Ordained in 1600, he then served at Rome, teaching theology and acting as secretary to Archbishop Lombard. Made vice-primate of Armagh in 1609, he reached Ireland in 1610. He held synods at Drogheda in 1614 and 1618.

Appointed Bishop of Ossory in 1618, penal laws forced him to seek consecration at Paris in 1620. His Analecta, first issued in 1616 and completed at Cologne, remains a famed defence of Irish Catholic history. He published lives of Saint Brigid and Irish histories, presided at Kilkenny in 1624, joined the Confederates in 1642 and greeted the papal nuncio Rinuccini in 1645.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doliche:
Doliche, a small city on the Germanicia-to-Zeugma road, was a titular see of Commagene. Its temple of Zeus Dolichenus brought it fame, and it minted coins of its own from Marcus Aurelius down to Caracalla. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets its ruins at Tell Duluk, three miles northwest of Aintab in the region of Aleppo. At an early date it became a bishopric answering to Hierapolis.

Lequien names eight Greek bishops, from Archelaus at Nicaea in 325 to Philoxenus in later councils. One bishop, Abibus, a Nestorian, was deposed in 434. In time Doliche itself rose to the rank of metropolis, and fourteen Jacobite bishops of the eighth and ninth centuries are also listed. The entry packs a long church history into a small city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elishe:
Elishe was a famous Armenian historian of the fifth century, dead in 480, whose birthplace and birth date are unknown. Some make him Elisha, Bishop of Amaduni, at the Synod of Artashat in 449. The commoner tale says he served General Vartan as soldier or secretary. That was in the war for religious freedom against Persia's Yezdigerd II from 449 to 451. Afterwards he turned hermit south of Lake Van.

Ancient writers call him vartabed, or doctor. His masterwork is the History of Vartan and of the Wars of the Armenians. David the Mamigonian asked him to write it. It tells how Armenians, Iberians, and Albanians fought together for their faith against Persia. It counts as a masterpiece of old Armenian letters, nearly free of Greek words. Good editions came from the Mechitarists at Venice, and translations exist in English, Italian, and French. An eighth chapter on later martyrs is questioned by scholars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-pasca:
Etienne-Pascal Tache, a statesman, was born at Saint Thomas, Quebec, on 5 September 1795, and died on 30 July 1865. In the war of 1812 he served as lieutenant of the Chasseurs canadiens. A self-made man, he graduated at Philadelphia as a physician after an elementary course, and later ranked foremost among Canadian statesmen.

Twenty-two years of medical practice came first, and then he entered politics in 1841 as a member of the Legislative Assembly, though he had opposed the Union. Re-elected in 1844, he took the post of adjutant-general of militia in 1846. In 1848 he became chief commissioner of public works in the Lafontaine-Baldwin ministry. Knighted in 1858, he was appointed aide-de-camp to the Queen in 1860, with the rank of colonel. In 1864 he formed the Taché-MacDonald administration and presided over the confederation conference of the British North American provinces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hippolyte-del:
Hippolyte Delaroche, also known as Paul Delaroche, was a French painter born at Paris in 1797 and dead in 1856. He trained first under Watelet, a landscape painter of modest ability, and then under Gros, a great painter but a poor teacher. The entry judges him badly trained, without deep insight into mankind or life and without a novel idea of art or beauty.

Yet Delaroche had a commonplace skill that pleased the public, and he shrewdly chose subjects to make up for what he lacked. His debut at the Salon of 1819 passed unnoticed, but a gold medal followed in 1824. He then settled into a long series of historical anecdotes, mostly from the civil wars of France and England. Multiplied by engraving, those scenes appealed to the bourgeois taste of the Restoration and July Monarchy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-melch:
Publicist Jacques Melchior Villefranche was born at Couzon-sur-Saône on 17 December 1829. He died at Bourg on 10 May 1904. After fine classical studies at Largentière's lesser seminary, he entered the telegraph service. In 1855, during the Crimean War, he directed the Varna telegraph bureau. Varna was the first landing place of Franco-Russian troops. In 1870, as telegraph director at Versailles, he served the Le Mans army's communications.

In 1875 he left the telegraph service and edited the Journal de l'Ain. There he defended religious liberty. His campaigns against school secularization laws were widely noted. His writing activity was very great. His Fables of 1851 and Fabuliste Chrétien of 1875 were welcomed in many schools. Historical and judicial romances from his pen were long read, notably Cinéas, or Rome under Nero. The entry presents a telegrapher turned Catholic journalist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-vegh:
Johannes Veghe was a German preacher and religious writer of the late fifteenth century, praised for his mastery of Low German. Born at Munster about 1435, he studied at Cologne. He entered the house of the Brethren of the Common Life at Munster in 1451. He led the Brethren's house at Rostock and returned to Munster as rector in 1475. Ill health led him to resign in 1481 and become confessor to the Sisters of Niesink, a post he held until his death in 1504.

Leisure for writing brought treatises such as the Spiritual Chase. It turns every detail of a hunt toward the search for God. The Marientrost treats devotion to the Virgin, and the Vineyard of the Soul treats progress toward perfection. His chief work is sermons preached in Low German before the Niesink sisters in 1492. They show keen observation of nature and the human heart in a vigorous, natural style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-beche:
John Beche, also known as Thomas Marshall, was an English Benedictine abbot executed under Henry VIII. Educated at Oxford and doctor of divinity in 1515, he ruled the Abbey of St. Werburgh at Chester and was elected Abbot of St. John's, Colchester, in 1530. With sixteen monks he took Henry's Oath of Supremacy in 1534.

The martyrdoms of the Carthusian priors, John Fisher, and Thomas More in 1535 moved him to speak with reverence for them, and spies reported his words. When he denied a royal commission's right to seize his abbey in 1538, he was sent to the Tower on treason charges, released, and rearrested. Tried at Colchester in November 1539, he stopped pleading against the new order, was convicted, and was executed on 1 December, receiving what the entry calls the crown of martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julius-peter-:
Julius Peter Garesché was a United States Army officer who died leading troops at the Battle of Stone River. Born near Havana in 1821, he studied at Georgetown College and graduated from West Point in 1841. He served on the frontier, fought in the Mexican War, and became assistant adjutant-general, ranking as captain, in 1855. He took an active part in Catholic life and helped organize Washington's first conference of the St. Vincent de Paul Society.

He also wrote often on Catholic, social, and political questions for the New York Freeman's Journal and Brownson's Quarterly Review. Pius IX made him a Knight of St. Sylvester in 1851. When the Civil War began, he declined a brigadier-general's commission and served instead as chief of staff to General Rosecrans. He was killed by a cannonball on 31 December 1862 while leading a column to regain a lost day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lecoy-de-la-m:
Richard-Albert Lecoy de La Marche (1839-1897) was a French historian. He trained at the Ecole des Chartes in 1861, served as archivist of Haute-Savoie, then of the National Archives' historical section from 1864. For years he also taught French history at Paris's Catholic Institute.

Gifted as writer and scholar, he never split historical truth from religious truth. His masterpiece, La Chaire francaise au moyen age of 1868, won a prize from the Academy of Inscriptions. It remains the standard work, studying medieval French preaching in three parts: preachers, sermons, and society as sermons reveal it. Kings, lords, bishops, priests, monks, burgesses, peasants, men and women pass through it with their traits and faults. Later books cover King Rene, St. Martin, manuscripts and miniatures, and thirteenth-century society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-francoi:
Louis Francois Richer Lafleche was a French-Canadian bishop and missionary, born in Quebec in 1818 and dead in 1898. Ordained in 1844 for the Red River country, he canoed 750 leagues to St. Boniface, then travelled 300 leagues more to La Crosse Island with Father Tache.

He mastered Sauteux, Cree, and Montagnais, and first set Montagnais into grammar. In 1851 he led the defence of sixty Metis against two thousand Sioux near Turtle Mountain, and the attackers withdrew after two days, awed by the missionary in surplice and stole. Later he taught at Nicolet, became Bishop of Three Rivers in 1870, and preached boldly on the social questions of his day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-vehe:
Michael Vehe was born at Bieberach near Wimpfen and died at Halle in April 1559. He joined the Dominicans at Wimpfen, went to Heidelberg in 1506, taught there in 1512, and earned his doctorate in theology in 1513. In 1515 he ran the Dominicans' Heidelberg house of studies as its regent. Cardinal Albert of Mainz later picked him for his theologian and put him in charge of the church at Halle in Saxony.

Called to Augsburg in 1530 to answer the Lutheran Confession, he played a leading part in the Leipzig debate with the Lutherans in 1534. Among his writings are pieces on Communion under one species, on honouring God and his saints, and the Assertio of 1537 on points the Reformers contested. These stand among Germany's best sixteenth-century apologetical treatises. Vehe also brought out a hymn book in 1537, and on 21 February 1559 he was called to the bishopric of Halberstadt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-niche:
A niche is a recess for a statue, designed to give it emphasis, frame it effectively, and afford some protection. It hardly existed before the twelfth century, and ranks among Gothic architecture's chief decorative traits. The constant, often lavish use of sculptured saints' images formed an essential part of the great style expressing the Catholic Faith, begun in Normandy through the Cluniac reform.

Once roughly chiselled bas-relief swelled into the round, detached figure, medieval builders learned a lesson Greeks had taught. Figure sculpture turns architectural only when incorporated with its building through surrounding forms harmonising it with the fabric. In Romanesque work the frame was little more than flanking shafts supporting an arch, the statue treated as accessory wherever flat wall appeared. The arrangement's convenience, propriety and beauty were at once apparent, and the niche's development as an independent form was constant and rapid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-maleb:
Oratorian thinker Nicolas Malebranche, born at Paris in 1638, built a philosophy in which God, not bodies, does the real work of sensing and knowing. Frail and home-tutored as a boy, he studied at the Collège de La Marche and the Sorbonne, turned down a canonry, and joined the Paris Oratory in 1660.

A chance reading of Descartes set his course, and his 1674 Search after Truth argued that sense and fancy serve practical need, not knowledge of things as they are. Later books refined that doctrine, and he died in 1715 after long disputes with fellow Cartesians and theologians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olivier-de-la:
Burgundian chronicler Olivier de la Marche, born in Franche-Comté in 1426, served Charles the Bold and his daughter Marie through war and court. Knighted by the count of Charolais in 1465, he became bailiff and captain of guards. Captured at Nancy in 1477 where Charles died, he ransomed himself to serve Marie as master of household.

His Memoirs, covering 1435 to 1492 and first printed at Lyons in 1562, remain singular and vital for the age, despite Walloon phrasing and long fêtes. Verse works include Le Chevalier Délibéré, read as his own life or an allegory of Charles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quiche:
The Quiche, also called Ulateca, were the chief aboriginal people of Guatemala. This encyclopedia entry places them in the great Mayan language stock, beside their neighbours the Cakchiquel, Pokonchi and Tzutuhil, whose four dialects form a single language. They held north-central Guatemala, including the present districts of Quiche and Totonicapan and part of Quezaltenango. Their traditions suggest a northern or north-eastern origin, and their fairly reliable history reaches back to about AD 700.

Pedro de Alvarado subdued them about 1525, with more than the usual atrocities, and they declined fast under slavery and heavy tribute. That decline came despite papal warnings and humane laws proclaimed by the Spanish crown. Brasseur de Bourbourg's studies of native languages, including the Popol Vuh, supply one source. Sahagún's history of New Spain and Squier's Central America supply others, on a people whose ancient books still speak for a shattered nation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-hyacint:
Saint Hyacinthe is the Quebec diocese, suffragan of Montreal. It was formed from parts of Montreal and Quebec by a bull of 8 June 1852 after a petition from the First Council of Quebec. At first it covered the south side of the Richelieu River and the Eastern Townships, land granted late in the eighteenth century to American loyalists. Later three parishes north of the river were added. It takes in the counties of Bagot, Iberville, Missisquoi, Richelieu, Rouville, and Saint Hyacinthe, with parts of Brome and Verchères.

Its city, a French Canadian town on the Yamaska thirty-five miles from Montreal, had 10,000 people. Jean Charles Prince, coadjutor bishop of Montreal, became its first bishop and took possession on 3 November 1852, turning the seminary into cathedral and residence. Fire destroyed it in 1854. He rebuilt, founded twenty parishes, brought the Sisters of the Presentation from France in 1853, and died on 5 May 1860.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sidron-de-hos:
Sidron de Hossche, in Latin Hosschius, was a poet and priest born at Mercken in West Flanders in 1596 and dead at Tongres in 1653. In youth he followed his father's trade as a shepherd, and at twenty he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Tongres. He soon showed a wonderful gift for Latin verse, and his first work, On Christ Suffering, in elegiac verse, appeared in 1635. Its chorus of praise brought him to the notice of Leopold William, Governor General of the Netherlands, who made him tutor to his two sons for two years.

Court life did not appeal to him, and he retired to Tongres until his death. His surviving works include On the Course of Human Life, On the Tears of Saint Peter, and many elegies and occasional verses. His age acclaimed him as worthy of the Augustan age, while sober criticism calls his works elegant versification.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-abban-of-m:
St. Abban of Magheranoidhe was a sixth- and seventh-century Irish saint, nephew of St. Ibar, apostle of Wexford and a predecessor and contemporary of St. Patrick. This entry makes him the son of Cormac, King of Leinster, flourishing between 570 and 620. And founder of many churches across Ui Cennselaigh, a district nearly matching modern County Wexford and the diocese of Ferns.

His chief monastery stood at Magheranoidhe, also rendered Murneave or Murnevin and later called Abbanstown, now Adamstown, while his abbey at Rosmic-treoin, or New Ross, grew famous as a school. He died on 16 March 620, and the entry warns readers not to confuse him with his namesake of New Ross.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-richard-de:
Richard de Wyche, bishop of Chichester, rose from a ruined estate to the chancellorship of Oxford and the episcopate. Born about 1197 at Droitwich in Worcestershire, he was second son of Richard and Alice de Wyche. He refused his elder brother's offer of the inheritance. He managed the family's broken property back to health. At Oxford he and two companions shared one tunic and gown between them for lectures.

After Paris and a master's degree, he studied canon law at Bologna and became chancellor of Oxford. Edmund Rich of Canterbury made him his chancellor and friend, and Richard backed the archbishop against the king over vacant sees. Elected bishop of Chichester, he reformed his diocese with energy. He died at Dover on 3 April 1253, famed for learning and sanctity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-didache:
Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, the Didache, is the early Christian manual recovered here. Some Fathers ranked it next to Scripture itself. Bryennios, Greek Orthodox metropolitan of Nicomedia, rediscovered it in 1873 in the codex that in 1875 yielded Clement's full epistles. Manuscript title reads Didache kyriou dia ton dodeka apostolon ethesin, with shorter heading Didache ton dodeka apostolon.

Three parts divide it: Two Ways, of Life and of Death, a ritual for baptism, fasting, and communion, and a section on ministry, with doctrine assumed rather than taught. Eusebius lists it among spurious books after Scripture. Latin version of chapters one to five, found by Schlecht in 1900, and the text's date, origin, and influence close a compact guide to primitive Christian life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-bathe:
William Bathe was an Irish Jesuit whose language primer shaped how Europe learned tongues. Born at Dublin in 1564, he died at Madrid in 1614. He went to Oxford about 1583 and while still a student issued a short guide to music in 1584, followed by a song manual in 1600. His skill on instruments, above all the Irish harp, won favour with Queen Elizabeth, to whom he was kin through the Kildare family, but his bent ran toward religious life.

From court he moved to Louvain for theology, entered the Jesuits at Tournai in 1595, and studied at Saint Omer and Padua. A 1601 mission to Ireland with the papal nuncio stalled in Spain, where he stayed. At Salamanca in 1611 he issued Janua Linguarum, grouping 1330 short sentences with Latin and Spanish face to face, plus a word index. Editions spread it to eleven tongues, and Comenius owned his debt to it in 1631.
cutler-lynch-law-an-investigation-into-t: Lynch-Law, an investigation into the history of lynching in the United States, by Cutler. The lynch-law history. This book preserves that study. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
dick-prescott-s-first-year-at-west-point:
Dick Prescott's First Year at West Point, or Two Chums in the Cadet Gray, by H Irving Hancock, opens the author's West Point series. Hancock's contents name the plebe year's stations. Two Tiny Specks of Nothing introduces the new cadets. The Tyranny of the Cadet Corporal and In the Hands of the Yearling Hazers follow. Greg's Case of Blues, a sudden grind at math, and Plebe Prescott's First Fight keep the pace.

Dick and Greg climb from candidates to class president by the final chapters. A prowler in quarters and a sentry's capture supply the mystery. The Saalfield Publishing Company issued the book in 1910. Hancock wrote boys' military series by the shelf. His West Point is exact about uniforms, demerits, and hazing rituals. Generations of American boys learned the Academy from him first. Some arrived at the real parade ground already knowing where to stand.
disturbances-of-the-heart-discussion-of-:
Oliver T. Osborne, an American physician, gathered his journal series on heart treatment into Disturbances of the Heart, a reference for doctors. A complete section on blood pressure marks the revised second edition. Osborne skips anatomy lectures and goes straight to therapy, how to treat each disorder at the bedside. The Journal's warm reception for the articles prompted the book form.

A classification of cardiac disturbances opens the work, sorting failures of muscle, valves, and rhythm. Blood pressure chapters treat hypertension, high pressure, and hypotension, its low opposite, as guides to action. Pericarditis, endocarditis, and chronic valve disease each receive handling, drugs included. Digitalis and other heart medicines of the era appear with doses and cautions. Diet, baths, acute heart attacks, and heart disease in children and pregnancy fill later sections. Medical historians read Osborne for a clear window on American heart practice just before cardiology tools arrived.
